one_liner: The original 2011 public-domain Ed25519 amd64 assembly in SUPERCOP. On Westmere it signs about 20x and verifies about 7.6x faster than OpenSSL-based P-256 ECDSA.
what_it_does: It implements Ed25519: EdDSA over the twisted Edwards form of Curve25519 with SHA-512, deterministic nonces, 32-byte public keys and 64-byte signatures. The code ships only as the crypto_sign/ed25519 directory of SUPERCOP. The page lists three interchangeable implementations: amd64-51-30k and amd64-64-24k (assembly) and a slow portable 'ref'. SUPERCOP has since added ref10, lib25519-amd64/ref10, neon and s2n variants. The API is NaCl's signed-message style: crypto_sign_keypair(pk, sk) with a 64-byte sk, crypto_sign(sm, &smlen, m, mlen, sk) producing signature||message, and crypto_sign_open. The amd64 code also has an open_batch entry point. It is a different scheme, key format and API from ECDSA, not a drop-in replacement.
how_it_is_fast: Field elements mod 2^255-19 use five radix-2^51 limbs. This avoids the slow add-with-carry chains that radix 2^64 hits on Nehalem/Westmere, and reduction is folded into the 25-mul schoolbook product through multiplies by 19. amd64-64-24k keeps radix 2^64 for CPUs such as K10/Core 2. Signing computes rB as a signed radix-16 fixed-base sum (Pippenger-style) over a 30KB precomputed table. Constant-time lookups load every candidate entry and combine them arithmetically, at a bit under 1000 cycles per step plus about 21000 for the final inversion. Verification merges the inversion into the square root when decompressing points, runs a double-scalar multiplication with a=-1 Edwards formulas, and compares encodings so R is never decompressed. Batch verification checks a random linear combination (128-bit z_i) with the Bos–Coster multi-scalar method over a heap using Floyd's bottom-up root replacement.
when_to_use: You want the canonical, public-domain Ed25519 code to study, benchmark against, or vendor into C on x86-64, and you control the SUPERCOP/NaCl-style glue (sha512, verify_32, randombytes)

Server-side verification of many signatures from many keys: the amd64 open_batch path handles up to 64 at a time. The paper measured under 134000 cycles per signature versus 273364 for single verification on Westmere
Designing a new protocol that is free to pick its signature scheme and wants small keys and signatures (32/64 bytes) and deterministic signing that needs no RNG

Side-channel-conscious signing on general-purpose CPUs: the authors state there are no secret-dependent branches or array indices, and SUPERCOP's goal files record a TIMECOP pass for amd64-51-30k (titan0, 2020)
when_not_to_use: Environments that must interoperate with ECDSA P-256 (X.509 PKI, FIPS-only policies, existing P-256 keys): Ed25519 is a different curve, key format and signature semantics, so there is no drop-in path
Non-x86-64 targets: both assembly variants are amd64-only (the 'architectures' file says amd64), and the software page calls the portable 'ref' 'slow'

Systems that need strict, consensus-grade validity rules. open.c rejects S only when its top 3 bits are set, so S values in [ℓ, 2^253) pass the check. Single verification is cofactorless (encoding of SB−hA must equal R), while the batch equation only guarantees 8SB = 8R + 8hA, so the two paths can disagree on crafted signatures
Production deployments that want a maintained library: this 2011 code is frozen, and SUPERCOP itself now carries lib25519-amd64, lib25519-ref10 and s2n implementations of the same primitive
Very long or streamed messages: the API takes the whole message in memory, copies it into the signed-message buffer, and for long messages the time is dominated by SHA-512

integration.dependencies: SUPERCOP/NaCl-provided crypto_hash_sha512, crypto_verify_32, randombytes and the crypto_sign.h namespace macros
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler plus an assembler for the qhasm-generated AT&T-syntax .S files (gcc or clang). The paper states no compiler; SUPERCOP's goal files show gcc -march=native -O3 builds
integration.platforms: x86-64 only for amd64-51-30k and amd64-64-24k; the portable C ref/ref10 run anywhere but slowly
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The C entry points read (keypair, sign, open, open_batch) keep their state on the stack, and keypair and open_batch call randombytes, so thread safety depends on that function

gotchas: The 64-byte secret key is the 32-byte seed followed by the 32-byte public key. crypto_sign copies A from sk+32 instead of recomputing it, so never assemble sk from a separately stored or untrusted public key
crypto_sign_open needs an output buffer m of at least smlen bytes because it uses it as scratch. On failure it sets *mlen to (unsigned long long)-1 and zeroes m

open_batch calls randombytes and caps batches at 64. It verifies fewer than 3 signatures one by one and, on any failure, falls back to individual verification. The paper's batch figures were the authors' own and were 'not yet benchmarked by' eBATS

The Westmere numbers come from the radix-2^51 amd64-51-30k code; the paper says radix 2^64 (amd64-64-24k) bottlenecks on Nehalem/Westmere. SUPERCOP selects the fastest implementation per machine, so which one you get varies by CPU
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over ENG25519 when you need plain x86-64 Ed25519 without AVX-512IFMA hardware, or when public-domain provenance matters more than peak throughput. libsecp256k1 and UltrafastSecp256k1 fit only when you need secp256k1 interop, and FourQlib only when a non-standard curve is acceptable.
verified_claims_summary: The paper (CHES 2011 / JCEN 2012) cites official eBATS reports on hydra2, a 2.4 GHz Intel Xeon E5620 (Westmere): 87548 cycles to sign and 273364 cycles to verify a short message. Against eBATS ecdonaldp256 (P-256 ECDSA; current eBATS shows it is an OpenSSL EC_KEY wrapper) at 1790936 and 2087500 cycles on the same machine, that is about 20.5x and 7.6x; the compiler is not stated. Current eBATS on 'alder' (Core i3-12100, SUPERCOP 20260831) shows the gap has narrowed. The fastest listed ed25519 is at a median of 27171 cycles to sign and 102613 to open, against 90965 and 248160 for ecdonaldp256 (about 3.3x and 2.4x).
status_note: Frozen 2011 research code (software page last revised 2017-01-22) that is still shipped and benchmarked in SUPERCOP 20260831. The promised NaCl integration never shipped: NaCl's latest release, 20110221, still ships a prototype crypto_sign and points to SUPERCOP. It is public domain and easy to copy for study, but a maintained descendant is the better production choice.
